question: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

Recent media reports1234 describe content creators using camera-enabled smart glasses to record public-facing workers and members of the public, apparently without their knowledge and without giving them a meaningful opportunity to object, before editing, uploading and, in some cases, monetising the footage on large online platforms. These cases raise questions about obligations under the General Data Protection Regulation5 (GDPR) in relation to identifiable footage captured by smart-glasses cameras, including with regard to transparency, lawful basis, fairness and personal data processing. Concerns are heightened where recording devices are not readily recognisable, recording indicators are unclear or can be obscured, and people are filmed in humiliating or confrontational situations, especially when those filmed are workers or others with limited ability to object. In view of the GDPR and, where relevant, other applicable EU rules, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does such processing of identifiable footage, including its recording, uploading, dissemination or monetisation, potentially trigger GDPR obligations for the recorder or uploader?

Without prejudice to the independence of data protection authorities, has the Commission engaged with the Irish Data Protection Commission, the European Data Protection Board or other authorities on GDPR principles for smart-glasses recording?

Will the Commission consider adopting EU-level guidance, standards or other measures in this area, including clearer recording indicators, anti-tampering safeguards, user warnings and effective platform notice-and-action procedures?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.7.2026) The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)1 provides that any processing of personal data must be fair, transparent and lawful2 and that data protection by design and by default is ensured3. Any natural or legal person acting as a controller or processor of personal data is subject to the GDPR. Data protection authorities have previously examined the compliance of personal data processing by means of smart glasses with the GDPR and have recommended measures to increase transparency for individuals4. The impact of such devices on individuals’ privacy and data protection has also been considered by the European Data Protection Board5. In addition, Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act, DSA)6 requires online platforms to provide users with easily accessible and user-friendly ‘notice and action’ mechanisms7, through which they can report content they consider illegal. Such notices must be processed in a timely manner and if the content is indeed found to be illegal, the online platform must remove said content expeditiously. Member States’ competent authorities and courts have primary responsibility for monitoring the application of the relevant legal provisions and for taking the necessary enforcement measures. The Commission is responsible for enforcing the DSA in relation to designated very large online platforms and very large online search engines. Supervision and enforcement of the GDPR falls within the competence of the national supervisory authorities and courts, without prejudice to the role of the Commission as guardian of the Treaties.
